readerTitle: Levi's went public twice. What does going public actually change?
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Levi Strauss & Co., Google, Dell) + 가상 적용 (가족 소유 의류 회사, 대형 소프트웨어 그룹 안의 사업부)
insight: 상장은 결승선이 아니라 거래다. 현금과 사고팔 수 있는 주식을 얻는 대신, 공개와 외부 주주의 압력을 받아들인다.
misconception: 상장하면 창업자가 한 번에 돈을 챙겨 떠날 수 있다. 상장은 성공한 회사의 최종 목표다.

sources.text: Levi Strauss & Co., company history (1971 listing, 1985 return to private ownership, 2019 NYSE listing)
Levi Strauss & Co. Form S-1 registration statement, SEC (2019)
Google Inc. Form S-1 (2004), "Letter from the Founders: An Owner's Manual for Google's Shareholders"
Dell Inc. go-private transaction with Michael Dell and Silver Lake (completed 2013)

factChecks.note: Levi's 연혁: 1971년 상장, 1985년 하스(Haas) 가문 중심의 차입 매수로 비상장 전환, 2019년 3월 NYSE 재상장. 게시 전 회사 공식 연혁과 2019년 S-1로 연도를 다시 확인하세요. 비상장 전환과 재상장의 '이유'는 카드에서 단정하지 않고 일반적으로만 적었습니다.
보호예수(lock-up) 기간 90~180일은 미국 IPO의 일반적 관행으로 적었습니다. 법적 의무가 아니라 계약 관행이며 국가·거래마다 다릅니다.
Google 2004년 상장 시 차등의결권(dual-class) 구조와 창업자 편지 문구 "Google is not a conventional company. We do not intend to become one."을 원문으로 확인하세요.
Dell의 2013년 비상장 전환은 사실로 언급만 했고 금액은 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 연도만 확인하세요.
분기 실적 공개는 미국 상장사 기준입니다. 국가별 공시 규정은 다루지 않고 '정기적으로'라고 일반화했습니다. 특정 국가의 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 했습니다.

cards.title: Levi's went public. Then private. Then public again.
body: Levi Strauss & Co. first sold shares on the stock market in 1971. In 1985, descendants of the founding family bought those shares back and took the company private.
In 2019, it listed again on the New York Stock Exchange. Same company, same jeans, two very different ways of being owned.

image.label: A pair of jeans walking in and out of a stock exchange door
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 청바지 한 벌이 증권거래소 회전문을 통과해 나왔다가 다시 들어가는 장면, 문 위에 "1971", "1985", "2019" 표지판. 실제 브랜드 로고, 빨간 탭, 거래소 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A bank says you could go public.
body: You own a profitable, family-run outdoor clothing company. A bank says you could sell 25% of the company on the stock market and raise a large sum for new factories. You'd still own 75%.
What is the biggest thing you'd be giving up?

options.text: A quarter of the profits, paid to new shareholders
options.feedback: True, you'd share future profits. But you'd also get cash to grow, so the pie may get bigger. That's not the deepest change.

options.text: Privacy and pace: strangers will see your results regularly and judge you on them
options.feedback: Exactly. You gain cash and a public price for your shares. You give up the quiet of answering only to people you know.

options.text: Very little. With 75%, you still call every shot
options.feedback: You'd keep voting control, but not the old freedom. Public owners, analysts and a daily share price now react to every choice.

cards.title: Two different deals with the world.
body: A private company has a few owners. It shares its results with them, and outsiders see little.
A public company can be owned by anyone. It publishes its results on a fixed schedule, and its share price moves every trading day.
Levi's lived under both deals. For more than 30 years it chose to stay private. Then it decided the public deal was worth taking again.

cards.title: Going public
body: **Going public** means selling shares in your company to anyone through a stock exchange. The first sale is called an **IPO**, or initial public offering.
It isn't really an ending. It's a trade: you get money and shares people can easily buy and sell, and in return you accept openness and outside owners for as long as you stay listed.

image.label: A balance scale: cash and shares on one side, a spotlight on the other
image.brief: 저울 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 접시에 "Cash", "Shares you can sell", 오른쪽 접시에 스포트라이트와 "Public results", "Many owners", "Daily price". 저울은 거의 수평.

cards.title: What you get, and what you give.

breakdown.label: Money to grow
breakdown.detail: New shares sold to the public fund factories, stores or hiring

breakdown.label: Shares that can be sold
breakdown.detail: Early owners and staff can turn shares into money over time

breakdown.label: Regular public reports
breakdown.detail: Sales, profits and risks are published for anyone to read

breakdown.label: Many owners, one scoreboard
breakdown.detail: The share price reacts to every result and announcement

cards.title: Founders rarely walk away on day one.
body: After an IPO, insiders usually agree not to sell their shares for a set time, often 90 to 180 days. Even after that, a founder selling a lot looks like doubt, and can push the price down.
So going public is less like selling the house and more like inviting new co-owners to live in it.
cards.softwareNote: Tech founders often protect control with two types of shares. Google's 2004 IPO gave its founders shares with extra votes, and their letter said: "Google is not a conventional company. We do not intend to become one."

cards.title: The public deal doesn't suit every business.
body: Listing costs money every year: audits, lawyers, investor meetings and management time.

It also rewards results that are easy to show every few months. A long, messy turnaround can be harder in public. That's one reason companies like Levi's in 1985 and Dell in 2013 went back to private ownership.
Many excellent businesses never go public at all.

cards.title: Now you run a unit inside a big company.
body: You lead the cloud storage unit inside a large, listed software group. Leadership is thinking about listing your unit as its own public company.
Your plan needs three years of heavy spending before it makes a profit. What do you recommend?

options.text: List now. We'd get our own cash and stock to reward the team
options.feedback: You gain money, focus and a strong hiring tool. But new owners would judge a loss-making plan every quarter, from day one.

options.text: List only once we can show steady progress each quarter and explain the long plan clearly
options.feedback: You get the benefits of listing without asking strangers to trust a plan they can't yet see working. Until then, the parent can be the patient owner.

options.text: List now, and keep the spending plan vague so investors stay calm
options.feedback: Public owners expect regular, honest reporting. Surprises later would cost far more trust than a clear plan costs now.

cards.title: Going public is a trade, not a finish line.
body: You get cash and shares people can sell. You give up privacy and accept many owners watching every result.
**Try it today:** list three decisions you made this year. Would each one look sensible if strangers read about it in a public report next quarter?
